issues.legal_issue: The prohibition on enforcing rights in benami property does not bar a recovery suit filed before the prohibition took effect, even if the suit remained pending when it took effect.
material_facts: The claimant filed her suit for a declaration of ownership and related relief on 30 September 1987, before the Benami Transactions (Prohibition) Act, 1988 came into force on 5 September 1988.
The suit was pending when the Act came into force.
The trial court dismissed the suit on the basis of Mithilesh Kumari, but the first appellate court later applied R. Rajagopal Reddy, which had overruled that decision.
issues.conclusion: The suit was not barred by Section 4 of the Act because it had been filed before the Act came into force; the High Court erred in disregarding the binding decision in R. Rajagopal Reddy.
issues.legal_principle: Section 4(1) bars the filing or entertaining of a suit, claim, or action to enforce a real owner's right in benami property after the provision takes effect; it does not make a pending suit abate. The Act creates substantive rights and liabilities and is prospective, not retrospective. The Court applied R. Rajagopal Reddy v. Padmini Chandrasekharan, which overruled Mithilesh Kumari v. Prem Behari Khare.

predicates.real_owner_benami_recovery_suit: A person claiming to be the real owner brings a suit to enforce rights in property held in another person's name.
predicates.suit_filed_before_prohibition_took_effec: The claimant filed the suit before the prohibition on enforcing rights in benami property took effect.
predicates.suit_pending_when_prohibition_took_effec: The suit remained unresolved when the prohibition took effect.

issues.definition: When a real-owner recovery suit is filed before the prohibition takes effect and remains pending at that time, the suit is not barred by that prohibition.

issues.legal_issue: A person who paid for property and was established as its real owner may prevent a named purchaser who contributed no purchase funds from conveying an interest without the owner's consent.
material_facts: The trial court found that the claimant paid the entire purchase price from her own funds, supported by evidence from a bank clerk concerning payment from her account.
The other person named as a purchaser claimed to have supplied half the purchase price through loans but produced no evidence of those funds.
That named purchaser sold a half share to another buyer without the claimant's knowledge or consent.
The finding that the claimant paid for the property remained undisturbed.
issues.conclusion: The claimant was the real owner, and the named purchaser's sale of a share without her consent gave the subsequent buyer no rights in the property. The claimant's ownership claim was valid and maintainable.
issues.legal_principle: On the established facts, the payment of the purchase price from the claimant's funds supported the finding that she was the real owner. The person named as a purchaser but shown to have contributed no funds had no right to deal with or sell the property without the real owner's consent. The Court relied on the undisturbed trial finding and the evidence supporting it; it cited no earlier case for this issue.

rule.if: real_owner_declaration_suit and claimant_paid_purchase_price and named_purchaser_contributed_no_funds and transfer_made_without_owner_consent

predicates.real_owner_declaration_suit: A claimant brings a suit seeking recognition of ownership against a person named in the purchase documents and a subsequent transferee.
predicates.claimant_paid_purchase_price: The claimant supplied the funds used to purchase the property.
predicates.named_purchaser_contributed_no_funds: A person named as a purchaser did not contribute funds to the purchase and did not prove that they had funds available for it.
predicates.transfer_made_without_owner_consent: The named purchaser transferred an interest in the property without the claimant's knowledge or consent.

issues.definition: If a claimant seeking recognition of ownership paid for the property and a named purchaser who contributed no funds transferred an interest without the claimant's consent, the transferee acquires no title.

issues.legal_issue: Whether a notice sent under a certificate of posting was served may be inferred from the circumstances, and a purchaser who received notice of another person's ownership claim before purchasing is not a bona fide purchaser without notice.
material_facts: The claimant produced a copy of a notice asserting her ownership, together with a certificate of posting, and sent it before the subsequent purchaser agreed to buy a share of the property.
The sender and intended recipient lived on the same road, and the agreement to purchase was made five days after the notice was sent.
There was no allegation or pleading that the claimant had procured the certificate of posting.
The first appellate court inferred that the notice had been served before the purchase; the High Court set that finding aside.
issues.conclusion: The circumstances supported a presumption that the notice was served before the purchase. The subsequent purchaser was therefore not a bona fide purchaser without notice, and the High Court erred in reversing the first appellate court's finding.
issues.legal_principle: Under Sections 16 and 114 of the Evidence Act, a court may infer from the ordinary course of postal business and the circumstances of the case that a notice sent under a certificate of posting reached its addressee. The inference is permissible, not mandatory, and may be rebutted or declined depending on the evidence. The Court referred to Harihar Banerji v. Ramshashi Roy, Ganga Ram v. Smt. Phulwati, Mst. L.M.S. Ummu Saleema v. B.B. Gujaral, M.S. Madhusoodhanan v. Kerala Kaumudi (P) Ltd., and V.S. Krishnan v. Westfort Hi-Tech Hospital Ltd.

rule.if: ownership_suit_disputing_purchaser_good_faith and notice_properly_addressed_and_posted and posting_certificate_produced and no_specific_fabrication_allegation and sender_and_recipient_lived_nearby and notice_posted_before_purchase

predicates.ownership_suit_disputing_purchaser_good_: An ownership suit disputes whether a purchaser acquired property in good faith without notice of another person's claim.
predicates.notice_properly_addressed_and_posted: The claimant addressed a notice asserting an ownership claim to the purchaser and posted it before the purchase.
predicates.posting_certificate_produced: The claimant produced a certificate of posting as evidence that the notice was posted.
predicates.no_specific_fabrication_allegation: The opposing party did not specifically allege that the certificate of posting had been procured or fabricated.
predicates.sender_and_recipient_lived_nearby: The sender and intended recipient lived close to one another.
predicates.notice_posted_before_purchase: The notice was posted sufficiently before the purchaser's transaction for delivery in the ordinary course to be inferred.

issues.definition: In an ownership suit disputing a purchaser's good faith, when a properly addressed notice was posted with a certificate, no specific fabrication was alleged, the parties lived nearby, and the notice preceded the purchase, the purchaser may be found to have had notice and not to be bona fide.
